name: Drizzle ORM
summary: A TypeScript library that declares tables in code and queries them through a typed API shaped like SQL, plus a relational API for nested data that always compiles to a single SQL statement.
intro: Drizzle calls itself “a headless TypeScript ORM”, and its pitch is “If you know SQL, you know Drizzle”. You declare tables with functions such as `pgTable`, `mysqlTable` or `sqliteTable`, and the column types flow into every query: `db.select().from(countries).leftJoin(cities, eq(cities.countryId, countries.id))` reads like the SQL it produces, and the result is typed to the columns you selected. There are no entity classes, no session and no change tracking; inserts, updates and deletes are explicit statements. Next to the SQL-like API sits the relational Queries API (`db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true } })`), which returns nested objects and, per the docs, always outputs exactly one SQL query, so loading relations can’t turn into N+1 round trips.

Drizzle Kit, a companion CLI, generates SQL migration files from changes to the schema, applies them, pushes a schema straight to a database, pulls a schema from an existing one and opens Drizzle Studio. The library has zero dependencies and targets serverless and edge runtimes. The docs cover PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite and services built on them such as Neon, PlanetScale and Turso, plus SingleStore, SQL Server and CockroachDB. The stable line is 0.45; version 1.0, with a second version of the relational API, has been a release candidate since April 2026. In March 2026 PlanetScale hired the whole core team to work on Drizzle full time.
strengths: Queries mirror SQL, so there is little new to learn and the generated SQL is predictable
End-to-end TypeScript types from the table declarations, without a separate schema language or code generation step
The relational API returns nested results in a single SQL statement, avoiding N+1 queries
Small, with zero dependencies, which suits serverless functions and edge runtimes
limits: No unit of work, identity map or change tracking: domain logic has to issue every write itself
Still before 1.0 in October 2026: the 1.0 release candidate changes the relational API and the upgrade needs a migration
Schemas are dialect-specific (`pgTable`, `mysqlTable`), so moving to another database means rewriting the table declarations

snippet.title: Declare two tables and run a typed left join on PostgreSQL
source: import { integer, pgTable, serial, varchar } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";
// select ... from countries left join cities on cities.country_id = countries.id where countries.id = 10
// rows: { countries: { id; name }; cities: { id; name; countryId } | null }[]

story: Drizzle started with Andrii Sherman, who in 2020 wrote an ORM called Drizzle in Java. Seeing the need for the same kind of tool in TypeScript, he and Oleksandr (Alex) Blokh pivoted it to TypeScript; the first code for `drizzle-orm` was written in 2021, and its first npm release came that September. Dan Kochetov later rewrote the library into the API it has today and built the first version of relational queries.

The team’s position was that tools like Django’s or Spring’s are better called data frameworks: you build a project around them. Drizzle set out to be a library you build with instead, staying close to SQL so developers learn one thing rather than SQL plus a framework’s API. The relational Queries API was added for the cases where SQL is awkward, such as nested results, while keeping the rule of one SQL statement per query.

For years Drizzle ran on more than 100 sponsors. In March 2026 PlanetScale hired the entire core team so they could work on it full time, with PlanetScale becoming its biggest backer. Version 1.0 entered beta in November 2025 and reached release candidate in April 2026.

choices.why: Other ORMs abstract SQL away, which the team saw as a double learning curve: SQL and the framework. Mirroring SQL keeps the full power of the database with almost nothing new to learn.

choices.choice: A library, not a data framework
choices.why: The team wanted developers to build projects with Drizzle rather than around it, so it has no required project structure and its tools are opt-in.

choices.choice: One SQL statement per relational query
choices.why: Nested results are where SQL-like code gets awkward, so the Queries API was added, but it always emits a single statement, which keeps round trips predictable on serverless databases.

choices.choice: Types from TypeScript declarations, zero dependencies
choices.why: Declaring tables in TypeScript gives types without a separate schema language or generator, and having no dependencies keeps it small enough for serverless and edge runtimes.
